paragraph.text: J25. "A party with only vegan food excludes people who eat meat"

it's the other way round. People who eat meat also eat rice, beans, salad, pasta, fruit and sweets without animal ingredients; vegans don't eat meat. A vegan menu is the only one everyone present can eat, so it's the most inclusive. Nobody goes hungry because there's no meat, and nobody is forced into anything: the party simply doesn't offer one kind of food.
"Making the school party vegan-only is an imposition. People who eat meat are left out."
At a party or group event, the menu should respect the preferences of the majority.
A vegan-only menu ignores that preference.
So a vegan-only menu excludes people who eat meat.

P1 is debatable: at a group event, the fairest criterion is that everyone can eat, not that the majority eats what they prefer. P2 is true. P3 is true, but ignoring a preference isn't excluding: people who eat meat can still eat everything that's served.
fails at P1 and in the step from "not having the preferred food" to "being excluded".
"A party without meat isn't a party."
"Vegan school meals are an imposition on children."
"Why does the office party have to be vegan if only one person is vegan?"
"The state can't ban what I eat." (which is E2)

At a party with egg-free chocolate cake, popcorn and veggie hot dogs, everyone can eat. If there were only food with meat, some friends would have nothing to eat. The party where everyone can eat is the one that includes the most people.

People who eat meat can eat vegan food, but vegans can't eat meat. That's why a vegan menu is the only one everyone can eat: it's the most inclusive, not the one that excludes. Nobody goes without food, nobody is banned from anything outside the event, and the party simply didn't offer one kind of dish.
"At the vegan party, who was left with nothing to eat?"
Vegans, vegetarians, people with some religious or health restrictions
Sometimes those who don't, for lack of dishes or cross-contamination

text.bold: 1. Not having your favorite dish isn't exclusion.

paragraph.text: Excluding means stopping someone from taking part. People who eat meat take part and eat normally at a vegan party.

text.bold: 2. Vegan food is the most compatible.

paragraph.text: It also suits vegetarians, many people allergic to milk or eggs, and several religious restrictions, such as those of people who don't eat pork or beef.
Outside the party, everyone still eats what they want. The event just chose a menu, as it always does.

text.bold: 4. Many everyday dishes are already vegan.

paragraph.text: Rice, beans, salads, pasta with tomato sauce, fruit, popcorn and many sweets have no animal ingredients.
Eating together matters for social life
A vegan party keeps the social side, with everyone at the table
The freedom to eat what you want isn't affected by a menu
(d) The strongest counter-reply: a party is also about tradition and pleasure
The most serious version says the barbecue or the meat dish is part of the party's tradition, and that removing it changes the meaning of the celebration.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: Party traditions change all the time.

paragraph.text: Menus change with the times, the place and who is there.

text.bold: Some people's pleasure doesn't outweigh everyone's participation.

paragraph.text: At a group event, making sure everyone can eat matters more than serving one group's favorite dish.
For the animals, a party with meat isn't a neutral tradition.
The question isn't whether the party became less traditional, but whether it's fair for animals to be killed for a celebration that can happen without that, and with everyone at the table.
J12 "I don't want to feel left out; eating together is how you belong"
Food as a way of belonging
E2 "The state can't ban what I eat"
The tradition of meat at parties
"Excluding" used to mean "not offering the favorite dish"
Calls excluding the only menu everyone can eat
The majority's taste becomes the event's obligation
And defends the menu that leaves some people with nothing to eat.
And accepts a meat menu being imposed on those who don't eat it.
And can eat everything that was served.
The usual menu seems neutral, and a different one seems like an imposition
Losing one dish weighs more than gaining others
The principle being tested is: "a menu without the dish I prefer excludes me".
It would exclude people who like soda
A peanut-free party, because of an allergic guest
It would exclude people who like peanuts
It's true that food is part of the tradition and pleasure of parties, that menu changes can bother people, and that the choice should be talked through.
But a vegan menu leaves nobody without food, and it's the only one everyone can share. It includes rather than excludes.
